The examples also use `Coder` and an Anthropic model, hence the `coder` and `anthropic` extras and `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`; swap them for your own tools and model provider. ## Set up the cluster Install agent-sandbox (v1.0.7 or later) with its extensions: ```bash kubectl apply --server-side -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/releases/download/v1.0.11/sandbox-with-extensions.yaml ``` Then define the pods your agent gets: - A `SandboxTemplate` describes one sandbox pod. - A `SandboxWarmPool` keeps a number of pods from that template started and ready, so a run doesn't wait for a pod to start. - Each run claims one ready pod from the pool. Deleting the claim deletes the pod. Each sandbox pod must run [sandboxd](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/tree/main/packages/sandboxd), agent-sandbox's in-pod server. Commands run in the container that runs sandboxd, so that container's image decides which tools the agent has. This template copies sandboxd into `python:3.12`, and the pool keeps three sandboxes ready: ```yaml apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: SandboxTemplate metadata: name: python spec: podTemplate: spec: automountServiceAccountToken: false securityContext: {runAsNonRoot: true, fsGroup: 1000} initContainers: - name: install-sandboxd image: registry.k8s.io/agent-sandbox/sandboxd:v1.0.11 command: [/bin/sh, -c, cp /usr/local/bin/sandboxd /sandboxd-bin/sandboxd] securityContext: {runAsUser: 1000} volumeMounts: [{name: sandboxd-bin, mountPath: /sandboxd-bin}] containers: - name: app image: python:3.12 command: [/sandboxd-bin/sandboxd, --root-dir=/workspace] env: [{name: HOME, value: /workspace}] securityContext: {runAsUser: 1000, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false} readinessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /v1/health, port: 8080}} volumeMounts: - {name: sandboxd-bin, mountPath: /sandboxd-bin, readOnly: true} - {name: workspace, mountPath: /workspace} volumes: - {name: sandboxd-bin, emptyDir: {}} - {name: workspace, emptyDir: {}} --- apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: SandboxWarmPool metadata: name: python-pool spec: replicas: 3 sandboxTemplateRef: {name: python} ``` For stronger isolation, set `runtimeClassName` (gVisor or Kata) on the pod template and [connect from inside the cluster](#connect-to-the-sandbox). ## Quick start ```python {names="defined"} from pydantic_ai import Agent from pydantic_ai_harness.coder import Coder from pydantic_ai_harness.kubernetes_sandbox import KubernetesSandbox agent = Agent('anthropic:claude-opus-5-5', capabilities=[KubernetesSandbox(warm_pool='python-pool'), Coder()]) result = agent.run_sync('Clone https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai and summarize how capabilities work.') ``` `Coder`'s shell and file tools now run in a sandbox pod claimed from the warm pool. For a narrower agent, use [`Shell`](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/harness/shell/), [`FileSystem`](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/harness/filesystem/) or your own tools on [`ctx.workspace`](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/core-concepts/workspace/#using-the-workspace-in-tools). - `Coder` creates it when the run starts, to load the repository's instructions, even if no tool is called. Pass `Coder(repo_context=False)` to wait for the first tool call. - It keeps running after the run, and is deleted 24 hours after it was claimed, whether or not anyone still uses it. Change that with `sandbox_timeout`, in seconds, or pass `None` to keep it until you delete it. See [Clean up](#clean-up). - Commands start in sandboxd's root directory, `/workspace` in the template above, and run as the container's user. - The image needs a POSIX shell with coreutils and `find`, since file operations run as shell commands. - Files are lost if the pod is lost. When a node fails, agent-sandbox starts a new pod that keeps only what the template puts on a persistent volume; the template above uses `emptyDir`. ## Continue in the same sandbox Pass the message history, and the next run works in the same sandbox: ```python {names="defined"} from pydantic_ai import Agent from pydantic_ai_harness.coder import Coder from pydantic_ai_harness.kubernetes_sandbox import KubernetesSandbox agent = Agent('anthropic:claude-opus-5-5', capabilities=[KubernetesSandbox(warm_pool='python-pool'), Coder()]) result = agent.run_sync('Clone https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai and summarize how capabilities work.') followup = agent.run_sync( 'Which capability would you add next, and where would it live?', message_history=result.all_messages(), ) ref = result.workspace.ref # or store this, and pass `workspace=ref` to a later run ``` `result.workspace.ref` is a `WorkspaceRef` holding `/`. Store it to continue later or to delete the sandbox. If the claim has been deleted, the run raises `WorkspaceUnavailableError`. Pass `workspace='new'` to start over. [Workspaces](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/core-concepts/workspace/#continuing-in-the-same-workspace) covers how runs find their workspace. The process that reattaches needs its own access to the cluster. `KubernetesSandbox` reattaches only to claims it made, as [Security model](#security-model) explains. ## Prepare a sandbox before the run To seed files before the agent starts, build the backend yourself, write through a `Workspace`, and pass the backend to the run: ```python {names="defined"} from pydantic_ai import Agent from pydantic_ai.workspaces import Workspace from pydantic_ai_harness.coder import Coder from pydantic_ai_harness.kubernetes_sandbox import KubernetesSandbox, KubernetesSandboxBackend agent = Agent('anthropic:claude-opus-5-5', capabilities=[KubernetesSandbox(warm_pool='python-pool'), Coder()]) async def run_in_prepared_sandbox() -> str: backend = KubernetesSandboxBackend(warm_pool='python-pool') try: await Workspace(backend).write_text('TASK.md', 'Add a `--version` flag to cli.py.\n') result = await agent.run('Do the task in TASK.md.', workspace=backend) return result.output finally: await backend.aclose() ref = backend.ref # set once the sandbox is claimed if ref is not None: await KubernetesSandbox(warm_pool='python-pool').destroy(ref) ``` The run leaves a backend you built open, so close it with `aclose()`. That closes the connection, including any `kubectl port-forward`, not the sandbox. To keep the sandbox, store `backend.ref` instead of destroying it. ## Clean up Delete a sandbox with the ref you stored. This deletes the claim, and with it the pod: ```python {names="defined"} from pydantic_ai.workspaces import WorkspaceRef from pydantic_ai_harness.kubernetes_sandbox import KubernetesSandbox async def delete_sandbox(ref: WorkspaceRef) -> None: await KubernetesSandbox(warm_pool='python-pool').destroy(ref) ``` A failed run returns no result, so delete its sandbox in an `on_run_error` hook: ```python from typing import Any import anyio from pydantic_ai import Agent, RunContext from pydantic_ai.capabilities import Hooks from pydantic_ai.run import AgentRunResult from pydantic_ai_harness.coder import Coder from pydantic_ai_harness.kubernetes_sandbox import KubernetesSandbox sandbox = KubernetesSandbox(warm_pool='python-pool') hooks = Hooks() @hooks.on.run_error async def delete_failed_run(ctx: RunContext[None], *, error: BaseException) -> AgentRunResult[Any]: if ctx.workspace.ref is not None: # Shielded so a deadline around the run can't cut the delete short, bounded so a hung call can't hang it. with anyio.move_on_after(30, shield=True): await sandbox.destroy(ctx.workspace.ref) raise error agent = Agent('anthropic:claude-opus-5-5', capabilities=[sandbox, Coder(), hooks]) ``` ### Find a lost sandbox If your program stops before it stores the ref, for example after a crash or Ctrl-C, the claim and its pod are left behind. To find it, search your logs for `Claimed Kubernetes sandbox /`, logged at INFO by the `pydantic_ai_harness` logger. Then delete it: `await KubernetesSandbox(warm_pool='python-pool').destroy(WorkspaceRef(provider='kubernetes', id='/'))`. ## Connect to the sandbox By default the client reaches each sandbox through `kubectl port-forward`, which suits running the agent on your machine. An agent running in the cluster connects directly: ```python {names="defined"} from pydantic_ai_harness.kubernetes_sandbox import KubernetesSandbox sandbox = KubernetesSandbox(warm_pool='python-pool', namespace='agents', connection='in-cluster-pod-ip') ``` - `'in-cluster-service'` connects through the sandbox's Service instead, which needs `service: true` on the template. - agent-sandbox's default NetworkPolicy blocks traffic from other pods, so add a `networkPolicy` to the template that lets your agent's pods reach TCP ports 8080 and 9090. - Port-forwarding doesn't work on gVisor or Kata, so use an in-cluster connection there. For other sandboxd ports, a port-forward that needs longer to start, or sandboxd started with `--auth-token-sha256` or `--auth-token-file`, pass the SDK's connection config: ```python {names="defined"} from k8s_agent_sandbox.models import SandboxdPodTunnelConnectionConfig from pydantic_ai_harness.kubernetes_sandbox import KubernetesSandbox sandbox = KubernetesSandbox( warm_pool='python-pool', connection=SandboxdPodTunnelConnectionConfig(grpc_port=9191, rest_port=8181, port_forward_ready_timeout=60), ) ``` `SandboxdInClusterConnectionConfig` takes the same ports, with `mode='in-cluster-pod-ip'` or `mode='in-cluster-service'`. Pass an auth token as either config's `auth_token`; every command sends it. ## Security model - `KubernetesSandbox` reattaches to and deletes only claims in its `namespace` named `pydantic-ai-` and 32 hex digits, the names it gives its claims. A ref naming any other claim raises `ValueError` before anything reaches the cluster. - The name is not proof of origin, and a `KubernetesSandboxBackend(ref=...)` you build yourself attaches to any claim it names, so keep refs server-side. - Your cluster sets everything else: - The pod's isolation. It shares its node's kernel unless `runtimeClassName` selects gVisor or Kata. - Which claims the agent's kubeconfig or service account can reach. - Which pods can reach sandboxd's ports. - Whether sandboxd requires an auth token. - The SDK talks to sandboxd over unencrypted gRPC. `connection='port-forward'` tunnels it through the API server. An in-cluster connection sends it over the cluster network as is. ## Configuration | Option | What it does | | --- | --- | | `warm_pool` | Name of the `SandboxWarmPool` to claim new sandboxes from. Required. | | `namespace` | Namespace of the warm pool and the claims. Default: `'default'`. | | `connection` | How the client reaches each sandbox: `'port-forward'`, `'in-cluster-pod-ip'` or `'in-cluster-service'`. For other ports, timeouts and auth tokens, pass the SDK's `SandboxdPodTunnelConnectionConfig` or `SandboxdInClusterConnectionConfig`. Default: `'port-forward'`. | | `sandbox_timeout` | Seconds after which a newly claimed sandbox is deleted. Default: `86_400`, 24 hours. `None` keeps it until `destroy(ref)`. | | `working_dir` | Absolute directory commands start in and relative paths resolve against. Default: `None`, sandboxd's root directory. Created on a new claim; on an attached one it must exist. | | `env` | Environment variables every command gets, on top of the container's own. Default: `None`. The agent's commands can read these, so leave out secrets it shouldn't see. | | `authority` | Who wrote the sandbox's files: `'none'` for files nobody on your side wrote, such as a cloned third-party repository, or `'user'` for the user's own. Capabilities that put a file into the prompt give it no more [authority](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/core-concepts/workspace-custom/#workspace-authority) than this. Default: `'operator'`, files you wrote. | | `path_authority` | An `authority` level for specific directories and files, overriding `authority` under them. The longest matching path wins. Paths are sandbox paths, relative to the working directory or absolute, and `~` isn't expanded. Default: `None`. | `connection`, `working_dir`, `env`, `authority` and `path_authority` also apply when you reattach; the other options only shape a new claim. ## Limits - Claiming or reattaching gives up with `TimeoutError` after 190 seconds. A claim that times out is deleted. - A timeout or cancellation kills the command's process group, not the sandbox. A job that detaches with `setsid` may keep running. - A background job that keeps the command's output open delays the result by about 5 seconds. Redirect its output to a file; `Shell.start_command` does this for you. - A command whose output passes 10 MiB is stopped with `WorkspaceOutputLimitError`. Redirect large output to a file. - While a lost pod is replaced, commands fail with an error durable execution retries. - The agent-sandbox SDK needs asyncio. Under Trio, every operation raises `UserError`. ## Durable execution Add a durability capability, such as `TemporalDurability()` from the `temporal` extra, next to `KubernetesSandbox()`. [Workspaces](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/core-concepts/workspace/#durable-execution) covers what changes. Outside a run, each command opens and closes its own connection, a new `kubectl port-forward` by default. So each activity takes a little longer than the same call inside a plain run. ## Telemetry `KubernetesSandbox` emits no spans of its own. Core's [instrumentation](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/capabilities/instrumentation/) records `pydantic_ai.workspace.provider` and `pydantic_ai.workspace.id` on the agent run span, and each command or file operation runs inside its tool call's span. ## API reference ::: pydantic_ai_harness.kubernetes_sandbox.KubernetesSandbox ::: pydantic_ai_harness.kubernetes_sandbox.KubernetesSandboxBackend

# Citations

A citation tells you which source backs up part of a model's answer: a web page it searched or fetched, a document
you sent, or a file in a provider's file store.

Pydantic AI puts citations on [`TextPart.citations`][pydantic_ai.messages.TextPart.citations], in the same shape for
every provider. The model's text is never changed.

## Turning citations on

Most models cite the results of search tools, such as [web search](native-tools.md#web-search-tool),
[web fetch](native-tools.md#web-fetch-tool) and [file search](native-tools.md#file-search-tool), without being asked.
Some providers only cite the documents you send, or on xAI any source, when you ask. So does Anthropic for web fetch,
and, on the Anthropic API, for web search on models with the `20260209` or `20260318` web tools
([Web Tool Callers](models/anthropic.md#web-tool-callers)).
Add the [`Citations`][pydantic_ai.capabilities.Citations] capability to ask them:

```python {title="document_citations.py"}
from pydantic_ai import Agent, BinaryContent, TextPart
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import Citations

agent = Agent('{{ anthropic:medium }}', capabilities=[Citations()])
result = agent.run_sync(
    [
        'How long do customers have to return an item?',
        BinaryContent(data=b'Items may be returned within 30 days.', media_type='text/plain'),
    ]
)
for part in result.response.parts:
    if isinstance(part, TextPart):
        for citation in part.citations or []:
            print(citation.sources[0].excerpts)
            #> ['Items may be returned within 30 days.']
```

The model can still answer without citations.

## Reading citations

A [`Citation`][pydantic_ai.messages.Citation] has:

- `sources`: where the information came from. A [`WebCitationSource`][pydantic_ai.messages.WebCitationSource] has the
  page's `url`. A [`DocumentCitationSource`][pydantic_ai.messages.DocumentCitationSource] is any other source. Its
  `document_id` is the provider's ID, not a file path, and a document you sent in the prompt may have no ID or title.
  Each source's `excerpts` are the passages the provider quoted as evidence. Several sources on one citation are the
  ones the provider grouped together; they may copy each other, so their number says nothing about how well the text
  is supported.
- `anchor`: the part of the text the citation is about, as character positions: `part.content[anchor.start:anchor.end]`.
    - A [`ContentCitationAnchor`][pydantic_ai.messages.ContentCitationAnchor] covers the text the sources support.
      Some providers, such as Anthropic, cite whole text parts, so the anchor covers the whole part.
    - A [`MarkerCitationAnchor`][pydantic_ai.messages.MarkerCitationAnchor] covers a marker the model wrote, such as
      `[1]` or a link.
    - `None` means the provider didn't say which text the citation is about. OpenAI file citations, for example, only
      give a position, which is kept in the part's `provider_details['citations']`.

```python {title="render_citations.py"}
from pydantic_ai import (
    Agent,
    ContentCitationAnchor,
    MarkerCitationAnchor,
    TextPart,
    WebCitationSource,
)
from pydantic_ai.capabilities import NativeTool
from pydantic_ai.native_tools import WebSearchTool

agent = Agent('{{ openai:medium }}', capabilities=[NativeTool(WebSearchTool())])
result = agent.run_sync('What is the tallest mountain in Alberta?')

for part in result.response.parts:
    if isinstance(part, TextPart):
        for citation in part.citations or []:
            anchor = citation.anchor
            if isinstance(anchor, ContentCitationAnchor):
                location = f'supports {part.content[anchor.start : anchor.end]!r}'
            elif isinstance(anchor, MarkerCitationAnchor):
                location = f'marker {part.content[anchor.start : anchor.end]!r}'
            else:
                location = 'somewhere in the text'

            for source in citation.sources:
                if isinstance(source, WebCitationSource):
                    label = source.title or source.url
                else:
                    label = source.title or source.document_id or 'document'
                print(location, label)
                #> marker '([example.com](https://example.com))' Mount Columbia
```

The same answer looks like this from different providers:

```python
from pydantic_ai import (
    Citation,
    ContentCitationAnchor,
    MarkerCitationAnchor,
    TextPart,
    WebCitationSource,
)

# Google selects the supported text, and here lists both sources for it. Anthropic's anchor covers the whole part.
TextPart(
    'Pydantic validates data.',
    citations=[
        Citation(
            sources=[WebCitationSource('https://a.example'), WebCitationSource('https://b.example')],
            anchor=ContentCitationAnchor(start=0, end=24),
        )
    ],
)

# OpenAI selects the link the model wrote.
TextPart(
    'Pydantic validates data. ([example.com](https://example.com))',
    citations=[
        Citation(
            sources=[WebCitationSource('https://example.com')],
            anchor=MarkerCitationAnchor(start=25, end=61),
        )
    ],
)

# Some providers give no position in the text.
TextPart(
    'Pydantic validates data.',
    citations=[Citation(sources=[WebCitationSource('https://example.com')])],
)
```

## Citations, tools and structured output

Citations are attached to text, so they only come back when your agent's output is text. With
[structured output](output.md), including an output type that combines `str` with a structured type, such as
`[str, Answer]`, the answer comes back as tool call arguments, which can't carry citations.

On Anthropic, and on Bedrock with Anthropic models, the model writes its citation markup into anything that isn't
text, such as `summary='<cite index="1-1">Items may be returned within 30 days.</cite>'`. So with
`Citations()`:

- **Structured output:** the model isn't asked for citations, so your fields stay clean and you get no document
  citations. (Anthropic rejects citations with `NativeOutput`.)
- **A tool call forced with [`tool_choice`](tools-advanced.md#dynamic-tool-choice-via-capabilities), in a request
  with a document or Web Fetch:** raises a `UserError` before that request is sent, because the markup reaches the
  tool's arguments every time. A run that forces a tool on a later step fails at that step.
- **Tools the model chooses to call:** citations stay on, but smaller models often write the markup into the tool's
  arguments, about half the time in our tests when the arguments summarise a document. Check arguments that end up
  in front of people, such as an email body, or leave `Citations()` off for those agents.

On xAI, the model answers in text instead of calling the output tool when citations are on, so with structured output
`Citations()` doesn't ask for them either. Tools work as usual.

If you need citations, use text output.

Anthropic cites [web search](native-tools.md#web-search-tool) results whenever the model calls the tool directly, so
with web search the markup can show up in structured output, with or without `Citations()`. The same goes for
[web fetch](native-tools.md#web-fetch-tool) when you set [`provider_settings={'anthropic': {'enable_citations': True}}`][pydantic_ai.native_tools.AnthropicWebFetchToolSettings.enable_citations] on the tool, which also has the model
call it directly on the Anthropic API on models with the `20260209` or `20260318` web tools. Results the model reads in code
execution come back uncited, and with structured output `Citations()` doesn't change which tools the model calls from
code execution; see [Web Tool Callers](models/anthropic.md#web-tool-callers).

On other providers, `Citations()` has no effect on structured output. With `NativeOutput` or `PromptedOutput` the
output is JSON text, so web search citations can come back on it, with positions in the JSON text rather than in your
fields.

## Good to know

- When streaming, citations can arrive after their text: at the end of each text part on Anthropic, Bedrock and
  OpenAI Responses, and at the end of the response on Google and OpenAI Chat. Read citations from the final response.
  On xAI they go on the last text part at the end of the response, so a streamed answer followed by a tool call gets
  none.
- The [AG-UI adapter](ui/ag-ui.md) doesn't send citations to the frontend.
- Citation URLs, titles and excerpts come from the sources themselves, and excerpts can include text from your own
  documents. Check them before you log them or show them to users.
- Anything else the provider returned about a citation, such as Google's confidence scores, is kept as the provider
  sent it in the part's `provider_details['citations']`. Its shape is the provider's and can change.

## Citations in message history

[Saved message history](message-history.md#storing-and-loading-messages-to-json) keeps every citation. When you send
it back to the same provider, these citations go with the text, so the model knows where its earlier statements came
from:

| Provider | Citations sent back |
| --- | --- |
| Anthropic | Web search citations, except on clients without web search, such as Bedrock |
| OpenAI Responses | Web and file citations, when message IDs are sent, which is the default for reasoning models. See [`openai_send_reasoning_ids`][pydantic_ai.models.openai.OpenAIResponsesModelSettings.openai_send_reasoning_ids] |

Every other citation stays on the saved messages, but its text goes back as plain text: document and fetched-page
citations, citations from OpenAI Chat, and history sent to a different provider. So does a citation whose text was
changed or joined with other text.

If you edit the text of a saved answer, also clear that part's `citations` and its `provider_details['citations']`.
Pydantic AI leaves out citations whose text clearly changed, but an edit that keeps the same length can go unnoticed.

History that's sent back unchanged goes out the same way every turn, so prompt caching keeps working.

The [Vercel AI adapter](ui/vercel-ai.md#citations) keeps citations when the frontend holds the message history.

!!! warning "The model may not see the source"
    If a user later asks about "source [1]", the model may see the `[1]` but not what it pointed to. Put the source in
    the new prompt, or let the model look it up again.

## Provider support

| Provider | Citations | How to turn them on | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Anthropic](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/citations) | Web search, web fetch and documents | Web search: always on direct calls, which `Citations()` makes the model use on the Anthropic API on models with the `20260209` or `20260318` web tools. Web fetch and documents, including documents returned by tools: `Citations()`. The `enable_citations` web fetch setting, [`provider_settings={'anthropic': {'enable_citations': True}}`][pydantic_ai.native_tools.AnthropicWebFetchToolSettings.enable_citations], turns them on for web fetch only | Anchors cover whole text parts. A fetched PDF is a document source. Citations of search results you provide yourself aren't included. On models with the `20260209` or `20260318` web tools, web results the model reads in code execution are uncited, as on a request that already needs code execution ([Web Tool Callers](models/anthropic.md#web-tool-callers)) |
| [Amazon Bedrock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_runtime_CitationsContentBlock.html) | Documents, on Anthropic models | `Citations()`, for text and PDF documents, including documents returned by tools | Other models on Bedrock don't support citations, so they ignore the setting. Anchors cover whole text parts. A document's title is the name Pydantic AI gives it, such as `Document 1`. Documents read from S3 aren't cited, as Bedrock doesn't allow it. With citations on, a text document must be UTF-8, or Pydantic AI raises a `UserError` |
| [Google Gemini API](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/google-search) | Google Search, file search and web fetch | Turn on the tool | Google Search URLs are Google redirect links, and titles are often just the site's domain |
| [Google Vertex AI](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/grounding/overview) | Google Search | Turn on the tool | Same as the Gemini API |
| [OpenAI Chat and Responses](https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/tools-web-search) | Web pages, and files on Responses | Turn on web search, or file search for files | Other annotation types, such as `container_file_citation`, are only available with [`openai_include_raw_annotations`][pydantic_ai.models.openai.OpenAIChatModelSettings.openai_include_raw_annotations] |
| [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/server-tools/web-search) | Web pages | Turn on web search. Perplexity Sonar models always search, and OpenRouter rejects them with the web search tool | OpenRouter doesn't say where in the text a citation belongs, so citations have no anchor |
| [xAI](https://docs.x.ai/developers/tools/citations) | Web, X and collection citations | `Citations()`, with a search tool such as web search or X search | Turning citations on changes the answer: the model writes Markdown markers such as `[[1]](https://x.com/...)` into it, and the anchor covers the marker. Collection citations are document sources |

# Migrate to Pydantic AI

If you have an application built with another agent framework, your coding agent can use a migration skill bundled with Pydantic AI. Each skill helps the agent understand the source framework, choose the right Pydantic AI components, and port one working application path at a time.

The skills preserve behavior rather than translating API names one for one. They separate responsibilities between:

- [Pydantic AI](agent.md) for agents, models, tools, outputs, messages, and streaming;
- [Pydantic Graph](graph.md) for explicit application control flow;
- [Pydantic AI Harness](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/harness/) for optional capabilities such as skills, memory, subagents, planning, and sandboxed tools;
- [Pydantic Evals](evals.md) for evaluation datasets and checks;
- your application for authentication, storage, APIs, UI, deployment, and other product infrastructure.

## Supported source frameworks

| Source framework | Migration skill |
|---|---|
| [LangChain and LangGraph](comparisons/vs-langchain-langgraph.md) | `migrating-langchain-to-pydantic-ai` |
| [Agno](comparisons/vs-agno.md) | `migrating-agno-to-pydantic-ai` |
| [Claude Agent SDK](comparisons/vs-claude-agent-sdk.md) | `migrating-claude-agent-sdk-to-pydantic-ai` |
| [Google Agent Development Kit](comparisons/vs-google-adk.md) | `migrating-google-adk-to-pydantic-ai` |
| [Mastra](comparisons/vs-mastra.md) | `migrating-mastra-to-pydantic-ai` |
| [OpenAI Agents SDK](comparisons/vs-openai-agents-sdk.md) | `migrating-openai-agents-sdk-to-pydantic-ai` |
| [Pi](comparisons/vs-pi.md) | `migrating-pi-to-pydantic-ai` |
| [Vercel AI SDK and Eve](comparisons/vs-vercel-ai-sdk.md) | `migrating-vercel-ai-sdk-and-eve-to-pydantic-ai` |

## Use a migration skill

Install the skills bundled with your project dependencies:

```bash
uvx library-skills --all
```

See [Coding Agent Skills](coding-agent-skills.md#library-skills) for installation details, including Claude Code support.

Then open your existing application in your coding agent and name the matching skill in your request. For example:

```text
Use the migrating-openai-agents-sdk-to-pydantic-ai skill to migrate this application
to Pydantic AI. Preserve its existing API and behavior, and verify the port with tests.
```

The coding agent should first trace a real request through the source application and record what callers observe. It can then migrate the smallest complete path, test the old and new behavior at the same boundary, and explain any difference that cannot be preserved exactly. Remove the old framework only after every required path has been verified.
